distillation_scope: First-layer disease manifold for acute catecholamine storm from pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma with hemodynamic instability and organ injury. Triggers, pregnancy, perioperative state, medication exposure, tumor hemorrhage, and definitive surgical timing are represented as axes, risk factors, or treatment modifiers rather than disease-id qualifiers.

evidence_basis.source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma
Endotext chapter on pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma
Pheochromocytoma multisystem crisis requiring temporary mechanical circulatory support narrative review

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Abrupt or sustained release of norepinephrine, epinephrine, and sometimes dopamine from a catecholamine-secreting chromaffin tumor. This is the upstream driver of paroxysmal hypertension, tachycardia, diaphoresis, metabolic stress, and end-organ injury.

Excess alpha-1 adrenergic stimulation causes intense arteriolar vasoconstriction, severe or labile hypertension, high afterload, splanchnic and renal vasoconstriction, and hypertensive emergency physiology.
Beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic stimulation drives sinus tachycardia, supraventricular or ventricular arrhythmias, tremor, hyperglycemia, lipolysis, and increased myocardial oxygen demand.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Catecholamine myocardial toxicity and stress cardiomyopathy
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: High catecholamine exposure, coronary vasospasm, tachycardia, and afterload mismatch cause myocardial stunning, myocarditis-like injury, Takotsubo-like dysfunction, pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Blood pressure lability with contracted intravascular volume
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Chronic and acute catecholamine excess contracts plasma volume, while vasospasm, myocardial stunning, capillary leak, sedation, and treatment can flip hypertensive crisis into hypotension or mixed shock.

Adrenergic hypermetabolism, tremor, vasoconstriction, and shock physiology raise temperature, glucose, lactate, creatine kinase, and oxygen demand; severe states can resemble toxicologic or endocrine hyperthermic syndromes.

Severe hypertension, vasospasm, arrhythmia, low-output shock, and microcirculatory hypoperfusion injure brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, and skeletal muscle, creating stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, AKI, pulmonary edema, and multiorgan failure hazards.

Tumor manipulation, anesthesia, surgery, labor, trauma, glucocorticoids, dopamine antagonists, sympathomimetics, monoamine oxidase inhibition, or unopposed beta blockade can amplify catecholamine release or unmask a previously occult tumor.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Accumulated injury from delayed catecholamine control
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Hours to days of uncontrolled catecholamine storm increase cumulative myocardial, neurologic, renal, pulmonary, and metabolic injury, raising mortality even if the tumor is later controlled.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: External stressors and tumor manipulation can acutely increase catecholamine release.
Perioperative or anesthesia timing is an observed context axis for trigger-amplified crisis.
Tumor palpation, biopsy, surgery, or embolic/hemorrhagic disruption may coincide with crisis onset.
Adrenergic, dopaminergic, glucocorticoid, anesthetic, or monoamine-interacting drugs can be the observed trigger.
Norepinephrine-rich catecholamine release activates alpha-mediated vascular constriction.
Epinephrine and norepinephrine activate cardiac beta receptors and increase chronotropy, inotropy, and metabolic output.
Adrenergic metabolic acceleration and muscle activity increase heat, glucose, lactate, and oxygen demand.
Norepinephrine excess is a direct biochemical expression of many pheochromocytoma crises.
Epinephrine excess contributes to tachycardia, hyperglycemia, and metabolic stress when secreted by the tumor.
Metanephrines reflect catecholamine metabolism and remain diagnostically useful even when release is episodic.
Twenty-four-hour urine fractionated metanephrines integrate catecholamine production over time.
Headache is part of the classic catecholamine paroxysm and may also reflect severe hypertension.
Sweating is a direct autonomic manifestation of catecholamine excess.
Patients often perceive beta-mediated tachycardia or arrhythmia as palpitations.
Cross-sectional imaging often reveals the chromaffin tumor substrate after biochemical or clinical suspicion.
Alpha-mediated vasoconstriction produces severe hypertension and hypertensive emergency physiology.
Marked systolic hypertension is a core observable of vasoconstrictive crisis.
Diastolic pressure rises with systemic vascular resistance.
Intermittent tumor secretion and treatment sensitivity produce rapid pressure swings.
Cool clammy extremities, mottling, or poor peripheral perfusion can result from intense vasoconstriction.
Severe pressure surges increase intracranial hemorrhage hazard.
Vasospasm, thrombogenic stress, arrhythmia, and hypertensive endothelial injury can produce ischemic neurologic events.
Beta-adrenergic stimulation rapidly increases heart rate.
Heart rate is a direct measured vital expression of beta drive.
Excess adrenergic tone lowers arrhythmia threshold.
Severe adrenergic stimulation and myocardial injury increase unstable ventricular arrhythmia hazard.
Catecholamines increase glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and insulin resistance.
Skeletal muscle beta stimulation produces tremor and adrenergic shakiness.
Myocardial injury, demand ischemia, and coronary spasm can raise troponin.
Catecholamine cardiomyopathy can sharply reduce systolic function.
Ventricular wall stress and pulmonary edema elevate natriuretic peptides.
High afterload, capillary leak, and systolic dysfunction can cause pulmonary edema.
Acute cardiomyopathy and hypertensive afterload raise decompensated pulmonary edema hazard.
Severe catecholamine cardiomyopathy can progress to low-output shock.
Vasospasm, volume contraction, myocardial stunning, and treatment sensitivity create large BP swings.
Crisis may present or evolve into hypotension from shock, myocardium failure, vasodilator therapy, or catecholamine depletion.
MAP can be very high during vasoconstrictive peaks and low during cardiogenic or vasodilated collapse.
Vasoconstriction, beta stimulation, and shock physiology can raise lactate.
Severe adrenergic crisis can produce fever or hyperthermia without infection.
Measured temperature tracks thermal stress severity.
Tremor, hyperthermia, ischemia, and shock can cause muscle injury and rhabdomyolysis.
Hypertensive encephalopathy, stroke, hypoxemia, shock, or metabolic disturbance can alter mentation.
Stroke or intracranial hemorrhage may produce focal neurologic deficits.
Renal vasoconstriction, shock, rhabdomyolysis, and multiorgan failure can produce AKI.
Renal hypoperfusion and muscle injury increase AKI hazard.
Shock liver, muscle injury, or multiorgan failure can raise AST.
Hypoperfusion or multiorgan failure can raise ALT.
Convergent brain, heart, lung, kidney, hepatic, and metabolic injury raises multiorgan failure hazard.
Persistent instability despite usual measures marks accumulating uncontrolled catecholamine injury.
Delay in catecholamine control raises cumulative risk across cardiac, neurologic, pulmonary, renal, and metabolic pathways.
Unstable ventricular or refractory supraventricular arrhythmias can cause sudden death or shock.
Low-output shock is a dominant short-term mortality pathway in pheochromocytoma crisis.
Severe pulmonary edema causes hypoxemic respiratory failure and can require ventilation.
Intracranial hemorrhage can be rapidly fatal or worsen through edema and herniation.
Large ischemic stroke during crisis increases mortality through neurologic injury, aspiration, and immobility.
AKI worsens acid-base, potassium, volume, and drug-handling risk in shock states.
Multiorgan failure is the final common pathway for uncontrolled crisis.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Higher pressure surges raise hemorrhagic neurologic risk.
Rapid pressure swings and vasospasm can impair cerebral perfusion and increase ischemic events.
Higher adrenergic heart rates reflect increased electrical instability.
Reduced ejection fraction increases low-output shock hazard.
Myocardial failure and high filling pressure increase pulmonary edema risk.
Hypoxemia worsens immediate mortality in pulmonary edema and shock.
High lactate marks severe adrenergic stress, hypoperfusion, and organ failure risk.
Rising creatinine tracks kidney injury severity.
Unstable rhythm can precipitate low output and shock.
Low renal perfusion during shock raises AKI hazard.
AKI amplifies acid-base, potassium, volume, and toxin burden in critical illness.
Multiorgan failure is a final common mortality pathway.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hypotensive or shock-phase crisis requires careful titration and parallel perfusion support.
Chronically contracted plasma volume can produce hypotension once vasoconstriction is relieved.

treatments.treatment_name: Titrated intravenous vasodilator blood pressure control

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renal failure affects choice and monitoring of some vasodilator strategies.

treatments.treatment_name: Oral alpha blockade with intravascular volume restoration

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pulmonary edema or severe cardiomyopathy limits rapid volume expansion.
Beta blockade before alpha control can intensify vasoconstriction and hypertension.
Low-output shock limits beta blockade intensity.

treatments.treatment_name: Magnesium sulfate catecholamine-release and arrhythmia modulation

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renal dysfunction increases magnesium accumulation risk.

treatments.treatment_name: Definitive adrenalectomy or paraganglioma resection after stabilization

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Inadequate alpha control raises intraoperative catecholamine and hypotension risk.
Severe shock may require bridge support before tumor removal unless source control is unavoidable.

treatments.treatment_name: Emergency tumor source control for uncontrolled complication

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Emergency source control may occur without ideal preparation and therefore carries high hemodynamic risk.

treatments.treatment_name: Trigger removal and catecholamine-provoking drug avoidance

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Known PPGL or adrenal mass greatly raises prior probability that a catecholamine crisis belongs to this manifold.
Functional tumor substrate increases biochemical catecholamine-metabolite burden.
Large tumor burden can increase secretion reserve and operative risk.
More secretory tumor mass may support more intense catecholamine exposure.
Procedural stress or tumor handling can precipitate abrupt crisis.
Procedural triggers often create rapid pressure swings.
Unopposed alpha effect can worsen vasoconstriction and hypertension.
Medication trigger can intensify hypertensive crisis.
Pregnancy changes imaging, pharmacologic, and surgical context but is not a disease-id subtype.
Labor, uterine compression, and delivery stress can trigger catecholamine release.
Limited cardiac reserve increases injury during catecholamine stress.
Structural heart disease increases shock risk.
Ongoing catecholamine exposure accumulates organ injury.
Treatment delay worsens short-term mortality risk.
Tumor hemorrhage or necrosis can trigger secretion and source-control urgency.
Structural tumor complication may be less controllable medically.
A young family history of adrenal or PPGL-spectrum tumor raises suspicion for hereditary tumor substrate.

supportive_care: Preserve the chronology of adrenergic paroxysm, blood pressure lability, heart rate/rhythm, medication exposure, anesthesia or procedural timing, pregnancy/labor context, tumor manipulation, and source-control timing.

Use presentation vitals, ECG rhythm, oxygenation, mental status, chest imaging, echocardiography, lactate, glucose, troponin, natriuretic peptides, creatinine, creatine kinase, liver enzymes, and catecholamine/metanephrine testing as ordinary evidence when available.

Represent infection, sepsis, thyroid storm, serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, withdrawal, acute coronary syndrome, stroke, and toxicologic syndromes through their own evidence paths without deleting overlapping fever, tachycardia, hypertension, altered mental status, or shock evidence.
Keep beta blockade timing explicit: beta control belongs downstream of adequate alpha control or tightly monitored ICU context, not as an isolated label.
For surgery, store alpha blockade adequacy, volume repletion, cardiomyopathy/shock state, resectability, rupture/bleeding context, and whether source control was deferred, staged, or emergent.
Trend blood pressure continuously when possible; single spot pressures can miss the lability that defines many crises.
Escalate organ support context for pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, malignant arrhythmia, cardiogenic shock, neurologic deficit, AKI, rhabdomyolysis, severe hyperthermia, or multiorgan failure.
